segments.text: Hey everyone, my name is Dr. Allison Hansen and I'm here at Gulf Coast Ultrasound Institute
for a hot tip of the day. Today we're going to be talking about ultrasound-guided fascia
iliacoplane block. Let's get to it. This plane block is performed with the linear probe.
Its indications are for femoral fractures as well as hip fractures. It's used for multimodal
pain control. Typically you start in the inguinal crease. Immediately you'll find your femoral
vasculature. Here's your artery, here's your vein. Just lateral to that. You see your hyperacoic
femoral nerve. As you slide more lateral, there's a hyperacoic fascial plane separating two muscle
bellies. In the far field is your large aliacus muscle and in your near field is your sartorius
muscle. This fascial plane leads you to your femoral nerve. And the great thing about this femoral
nerve plane block is that you're not actually dumping anesthetic at the nerve. You are dumping
the anesthetic in between this fascial plane. It's very safe and generally very easy to do.
Your in-plane technique, trajectory is lateral to medial. You should be able to visualize
the long axis of your needle coming in. As soon as you feel a pop underneath that fascial
plane, you'll deliver one to two CCs of either normal saline to hydrodysect or your preferred
anesthetic.
As you see the anesthetic or normal saline unzip that facial plane, you'll know that you're
in the right place.
If you see anesthetic bubbling up, you're likely in the musculature, you need to either
proceed deeper with your needle or pull back and give another one to two CCs testos.
If you're in the right place, again, you'll see the fascia, unzip, as well as depression
of the iliacus muscle.
That was your hot tip of the day.
Now you go give it a try.
